title: Vectors
short: A vector has a size and a direction.
trouble: Students treat a vector's components as a point rather than as a displacement.

blocks.html: "Walk $5$ km" is not enough to find your way; you need "walk $5$ km northeast." Quantities like displacement, velocity and force have both a size and a direction. Your work with angles will help describe the direction.

A vector has a magnitude (length) and a direction, and is drawn as an arrow. In component form, $\mathbf{v} = \langle a, b \rangle$ means "move $a$ across and $b$ up." The vector from $P(x_1, y_1)$ to $Q(x_2, y_2)$ is $$\overrightarrow{PQ} = \langle x_2 - x_1,\ y_2 - y_1 \rangle.$$ Arrows with the same length and direction are the same vector, wherever they start.

A vector records a move, not a place. "Three right and four up" is the same instruction whether you start at your door or across town; only the starting point differs. That is why a vector can slide anywhere without changing, and why subtraction (end minus start) gives its components.

blocks.name: vectors2d
blocks.cap: Drag the tip of the arrow. Its components are the horizontal and vertical parts of the move.

blocks.title: Where does it end?
blocks.q: The vector $\langle -2, 5 \rangle$ starts at $(3, 1)$. Where does it end?
steps: Make the move from the starting point: $x$: $3 + (-2) = 1$, $y$: $1 + 5 = 6$.

blocks.title: Same vector?
blocks.q: Do the arrows from $(0, 0)$ to $(2, 3)$ and from $(4, 1)$ to $(6, 4)$ represent the same vector?
steps: Same move, so the same vector, drawn in two places.

blocks.html: Treating the components $\langle 3, 4 \rangle$ as the point $(3, 4)$. They match only when the arrow starts at the origin. If the arrow starts at $(1, 1)$, it ends at $(4, 5)$. Think "move," not "location." The angle brackets are a reminder of that difference.

Vectors are written in bold ($\mathbf{v}$) or with an arrow ($\vec{v}$). Another common form uses the unit vectors $\mathbf{i} = \langle 1, 0 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{j} = \langle 0, 1 \rangle$: $\langle 3, -4 \rangle = 3\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j}$.
